title: Water Heater Relief (T&P) Valve Dripping or Leaking: Causes & Fixes
question: Why is my water heater's temperature/pressure-relief valve dripping water from the discharge pipe, and how do I fix it?
summary: A water heater relief (T&P) valve that drips is usually reacting to pressure, not a broken valve. The most common cause is thermal expansion on a closed plumbing system (a pressure-reducing valve, check valve, or backflow preventer on the main and no expansion tank), followed by too-high house water pressure, too-high temperature, or a worn valve that no longer seals. The fixes (an expansion tank, a pressure-gauge check, lowering the temperature to 120°F, or swapping the ~$20 valve) are mostly DIY. Two hard rules: never cap or plug the valve or its discharge pipe (that can turn the tank into a bomb), and if the discharged water is steaming or the valve is gushing, the valve is doing its job against a real overheat: shut the heater off and call a plumber.

commonCauses.cause: Thermal expansion on a closed system: when the burner or element heats the water it expands, and if a pressure-reducing valve, check valve, or backflow preventer on the main blocks it from pushing back into the city line, pressure climbs and the valve weeps. The most common modern cause.
commonCauses.quickCheck: The drip appears shortly after the heater recovers (a shower, dishwasher, or overnight heat-up), and you have a PRV/check valve/backflow preventer on the main but no thermal expansion tank near the heater.

commonCauses.cause: House water pressure too high (over ~80 psi): the incoming supply itself is over the code limit, so normal heating pushes the tank past the valve's 150 psi trip point.
commonCauses.quickCheck: Screw a $10-15 pressure gauge onto a hose bib or the laundry faucet; a static reading over 80 psi points to needing a pressure-reducing valve.

commonCauses.cause: Temperature set too high (or a failing thermostat/gas control letting the water overheat): the water reaches the valve's 210°F temperature trip.
commonCauses.quickCheck: Check the setting; if it's above ~130-140°F or the hot water runs scalding/steaming, lower it to 120°F and watch whether the drip stops.

commonCauses.cause: Worn, mineral-fouled, or not-reseated valve: the valve seat is pitted or has grit and no longer seals, or it started dripping right after someone flipped the test lever and it didn't snap back shut.
commonCauses.quickCheck: It weeps continuously no matter when the heater runs, or the drip began immediately after the test lever was lifted.

commonCauses.cause: The valve is correctly warning of an overheat/overpressure (runaway heating from a stuck thermostat or gas control), the least common but the dangerous case.
commonCauses.quickCheck: The discharged water is steaming-hot, the tank rumbles/percolates, or the valve is discharging heavily; treat it as an emergency, not a valve swap.

fixes: First figure out which drip you have. Watch when it happens: a drip right after the heater reheats a big draw = thermal expansion or high pressure; a constant weep = a worn valve; steaming water or a gushing valve = a real overheat (skip to the emergency step). Also confirm the water is truly from the T&P valve/discharge pipe, not a fitting above it.

Lower the temperature. Set a gas heater's dial or both electric thermostats to about 120°F, wait a day, and see if the dripping stops. 120°F is the recommended setpoint for scald and energy reasons anyway, and too-high temperature is a common trigger.

Test your water pressure. Thread a $10-15 gauge onto a hose bib or the laundry faucet; static house pressure should read under 80 psi. If it's high, or you have a pressure-reducing valve, check valve, or backflow preventer on the main, expansion has nowhere to go when the water heats, the classic weep cause.

Add a thermal expansion tank if you have a closed system. Install a properly pre-charged expansion tank (pre-charge set to match your house pressure) on the cold supply near the heater. It absorbs the expansion and is the real fix for thermal-expansion weeping, a manageable DIY plumbing job if you're comfortable working on supply lines; otherwise hire a plumber.
Have a pressure-reducing valve installed if incoming pressure is over 80 psi. This is usually a plumber job on the main line and is often required by code above 80 psi.

Exercise the valve to clear grit, knowing the risk. With a bucket under the discharge pipe and your hand clear of the hot stream, briefly lift the test lever to flush the seat, then let it snap shut. On an old valve this can make the drip worse because it won't reseat; if so, replace it.

Replace the T&P valve if it weeps constantly or won't reseat. Set the gas control to OFF/pilot or switch the breaker OFF, close the cold-water inlet, drain a few gallons so the level is below the valve, remove the discharge pipe, unscrew the old valve, and thread in a new one rated 150 psi / 210°F with Teflon tape. Reattach the discharge pipe. The valve is a $15-40 part.

Never cap, plug, or put a shutoff on the valve or its discharge pipe, and keep the discharge pipe code-correct: same size as the valve outlet, rigid pipe rated for hot water, sloped continuously downhill, no threads on the end, terminating within about 6 inches of the floor or a drain. Blocking it can build the tank to a rupture.

Emergency: if the water is steaming/scalding, the valve is gushing, or the tank rumbles or percolates, the valve is warning of a real overheat. Shut the heater off (gas control to OFF, or breaker OFF), close the cold inlet, stay clear of the hot discharge, and call a plumber right away; do not just replace the valve.
diyVsPro: Most of the diagnosis and the common fixes are DIY: lowering the temperature, testing water pressure with a gauge, exercising the valve, and swapping the T&P valve itself are homeowner-level jobs (the valve is a ~$20 threaded part). Installing a thermal expansion tank is a moderate DIY plumbing job if you're comfortable working on supply lines. Call a licensed plumber to install or adjust a pressure-reducing valve on your main, and always for the dangerous case: a heater that is actually overheating (steaming water, rumbling tank, gushing valve), which points to a failed thermostat or gas control, not a bad valve. On a gas heater, leave anything touching the gas line or control valve to the pro; you can still set the control to OFF/pilot to service the T&P valve yourself.
typicalCostUSD: DIY parts: T&P relief valve $15-40; water pressure gauge $10-15; thermal expansion tank $40-90; Teflon tape and fittings a few dollars. Pro: plumber service call $100-250; T&P valve replaced $150-350 installed; thermal expansion tank installed $150-350; pressure-reducing valve installed $250-450; diagnosing/repairing an overheating heater (thermostat or gas control) $150-500+.
timeEstimate: Lowering the temperature or testing pressure: 10-20 minutes, plus waiting a day to see if the drip stops. Replacing the T&P valve: 30-60 minutes including draining a few gallons. Installing an expansion tank: 1-2 hours. A plumber typically handles any of these in a single visit.
safetyNote: The T&P valve is a critical over-pressure and over-temperature safeguard: NEVER cap, plug, or install a shutoff on it or its discharge pipe; a blocked valve can let the tank build to a rupture (a steam explosion). If the discharged water is steaming or scalding, the valve is gushing, or the tank rumbles/percolates, the heater is overheating: shut it off (gas control OFF, or breaker OFF), close the cold inlet, stay clear of the hot stream, and call a plumber immediately. Relief water can be 150-210°F and will burn you. For a GAS heater, do not work on the gas line or control valve; set the control to OFF/pilot to service the valve, and if you smell gas, leave the house and call your gas utility from outside. For an ELECTRIC heater, switch the 240V breaker OFF before servicing and never run an element dry. Keep the discharge pipe rigid, unthreaded at the end, sloped downward, and ending within about 6 inches of the floor or a drain.
toolsParts: Replacement T&P relief valve (rated 150 psi / 210°F, matching your tank's threads, usually 3/4 in)
Pipe wrench or large channel-lock pliers
Thermal expansion tank (if you have a closed system)
Rigid CPVC or copper pipe and fittings for the discharge line (if replacing it)
Garden hose (to drain the tank below the valve)
Screwdriver (to reach electric thermostats / adjust the setting)
